title: Conserved carbon density in marine picocyanobacteria improves phytoplankton biomass estimates
content:
Abstract

The picocyanobacteria Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus dominate oligotrophic oceans, where nitrogen (N) limitation is pervasive, and contribute substantially to marine primary production. However, their carbon biomass remains poorly constrained due to their extremely small cell size and the scarcity of direct measurements. Existing estimates largely rely on cellular carbon quota (Q C) or carbon density derived from nutrient-replete laboratory cultures, which may not reflect the sustained N-limited conditions typical of oligotrophic oceans. Here, we established N-limited chemostat systems to investigate how Q C and cell size respond to different degrees of N limitation in Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus. Synechococcus exhibited gradual declines in both cell volume and Q C with increasing N limitation. In contrast, Prochlorococcus showed an initial sharp reduction followed by stabilization, suggesting that it may have approached physiological lower limits in cell volume and Q C. These results indicate a close coupling between cell size and Q C in both genera under N limitation. Compilation of data from this and previous studies further showed that both genera maintained a nearly constant organic carbon density of ~ 246 fg C μm−3 across strains and environmental conditions, including variations in nutrient supply, light intensity, and temperature. This conserved carbon density provides a simple and reliable conversion factor for estimating picocyanobacterial carbon biomass. By integrating datasets from picocyanobacteria and eukaryotic phytoplankton, we also developed a universal C : vol model spanning a broad cell size spectrum (10−1–107 μm3). Together, these findings improve estimates of marine phytoplankton carbon biomass and provide improved constraints for marine biogeochemical models.
